What impact is AI having? I'm of the view that we should be focussing more on aggregate outputs, relatively less on inputs or intermediate proxies.

- Inputs: time spent across different activities; money spent on tokens.

- Intermediate proxies: working papers; lines of code, commits & pull requests; self-reported speedup. 

- Final outputs: total cyber exploits discovered; total math problems solved; algorithmic efficiency.

The disadvantage of inputs & intermediate proxies is that they're very hard to interpret -- totally possible that they move, but outputs don't, and vice versa. Lines of code could explode without value changing; and vice versa.

A disadvantage of final outputs is (1) it's harder to run experiments; (2) it's hard to attribute to whether the change is AI or not. But in some domains the trend-break is so large that it's *obviously* AI.

Q: has AI accelerated aggregate discovery yet?

My very general impresions, would love others' thoughts:

1. Vulnerability discovery is up a lot. Between 2X-5X increase in volume, although the average severity has fallen somewhat.

2. Algorithmic efficiency hasn't moved much. E.g. nanogpt, SAT solvers, compression efficiency, chess algorithmic ability. They haven't shown noticeable changes I believe.

3. Math is hard to judge. Erdős problems are certainly falling faster than historical rates, but it's mainly the obscure ones. We don't seem to be tightening upper and lower bounds on unknown quantities noticeably more quickly AFAICT. There are some prominent AI discoveries (e.g. unit distance) but I don't know what's the denominator, i.e. the average flow of comparably important results, my guess is it's still small.

4. Papers/code volume is up a lot.  Total arXiv papers and github code is up a lot, but no good way of judging how the quality has changed.

TLDR: the apple-picking model says Mythos will have a moderate impact on AI R&D, but a big impact on cybersecurity.

How do we quantify a model's ability to push the frontier? E.g. progress in finding new bugs, proving new theorems, finding new optimizations.

The apple-picking model implies you can benchmark against human-equivalent-time, e.g. you can say a model can advance the frontier by the equivalent of a human-week. 

But importantly the time-horizons are not additive. You can stack human weeks, you can't stack agent-weeks, because agents systematically pluck all the low-hanging fruit.

This has pretty different implications for different domains:

- The AI R&D stack has a small number of critical algorithms, so adding an additional 1-month of human effort to each algorithm doesn't help you a great deal.

- The cybersecurity landscape has tens of thousands of potential attack surfaces, so deploying agents in parallel to expand a human-month of effort to attack or defend those surfaces has a huge impact.

Concretely: AI R&D is a few tall narrow trees, already pretty well-picked; cybersecurity is a huge orchard with a ton of low-hanging fruit.

It's fiddly to keep having to copy-and-paste to another document, or to tweak prompts and wait for a new response.

1. Get o3 to compile a scrapbook file (a list of URLs satisfying some criteria, and the entire content of each URL, or long verbatim quotes, in markdown format).

1907190254010044883.text:
One nice model of LLMs is that they make private knowledge public.

I haven't seen an economic model written down in quite this form, is there a reference I'm missing?

Suppose each person has a given level of productivity at each task, which reflects their knowledge, and represents their comparative advantage. Now suppose the introduction of LLMs makes all that private knowledge public: you have a device in your pocket that can give you advice that you'd normally get from a doctor, electrician, lawyer, accountant.

This has a number of implications:

1. Wages will fall in highly-paid professions.

2. We will produce relatively more of the things where knowledge is a scarce input (and so wages are high): medicine, engineering, law.

3. The returns to experience within an occupation will flatten, and so inequality within occupations should fall.

4. Those who have skills that are complements to knowledge (e.g. intelligence) will have relatively bigger lifts in productivity.

5. People will exchange less on the market (GDP could fall) because they can do more themselves.

6. The incentives to discover new knowledge will weaken.

Even physical jobs would be affected. Strawberry pickers, baristas, arborists, can ask an LLM how to solve a problem, or can ask a multimodal model to critique their form.

This observation would also apply to books and the internet: they have dramatically changed the distribution of information and should've had similar flattening effects.

Driving down the 5 from SF to LA and I keep checking the car's estimate of how long until we arrive, hoping with each glance for it to go down quicker.

At some point I stop paying attention to the time remaining and start looking at the time elapsed. I realize I'm now wishing for it to move slower not faster. 

My wife & daughter are asleep in the back seat, my mind is wandering, the road is clear, it's a pleasure, I don't want this to end.

Like being happy to see there are only 10 pages left in my book then suddenly sad when I remember it's a good book.

The hours are slow & the years quick.

Like an octopus pulling on the bars of its cage alternately from the inside and the outside.

On a lunch break at a summer school in Trento I bought a watch because I didn't want to check the time on my phone during boring talks. It didn't make the talks go any faster and I wouldn't have wanted them to -- better to find out I have 10 minutes more of a boring lecture than to find out I have 10 minutes less of life.

Finally we want a theory of why some metrics are accelerating and some not. What types of discovery is AI particularly good at helping with?

Here's a very loose conjecture: AI accelerates discovery where the marginal cost of an experiment is low. If experiments (AKA verifications) are cheap, then you can use experiments as a substitute for understanding; if they're expensive you still need to lean on human understanding. I will make some very conjectural claims about the marginal cost of experiments/verifications in different areas:

- Cyber vulnerabilities: marginal cost is small once you already have the software loaded in memory, a few CPU cycles to verify. 

- Math proofs/counterexamples: the fixed cost of formalizing a problem can be high (e.g. converting to Lean, or expressing the core problem in code), but the marginal cost is just a few CPU cycles.

- NanoGPT: until recently the cost of a single run was 8xH100 GPU for 1.5 minutes, and to get tight confidence intervals you need 18 of those runs. This could perhaps explain why we didn't get much movement until recently.

- Hutter compression: 50 hours of CPU time.

- Stockfish: Claude estimates $100-300 of compute cost to statistically verify a small improvement.

- CIFAR: Claude says it's ~$1 to verify, so this could be a counterexample.

An implication of this theory: we might see slower curve-bending in domains where the cost of experimentation is large, e.g. frontier pretraining, where experiments can cost a huge amount of money; and domains where we need real-world experiments -- physics, chemistry, biology (though everything changes if we can trust simulations).

Also note a corollary of this theory: if data and intelligence are substitutes, then making our AI smarter will loosen the bottleneck from experiments.

2107188675398553720.text:
Overall I think this is evidence of a lot more curve-bending in the last 6 weeks, and the algorithmic progress should be updating for people who worry about RSI.

A reminder: (1) we're looking at metrics with a reasonable pre-AI baseline rate of discovery, and (2) this update only discusses metrics we already discussed in the previous post.

Some additional observations:

1. The most important curves are secret. We really want to know when the frontier labs' AI efficiency and capability curves start bending, and that's not generally public information.

2. I think this area is under-invested in. I'd love to see people maintaining dashboards of curves to watch for when they start bending. I'm confident the set of metrics I'm tracking could be substantially improved. I find this information much more updating than results from LLM benchmarks or RCTs.

3. Whether the discoveries are AI-alone or AI-assisted is always hard to tell, but it matters less than the aggregate rate of discoveries.

4. What other metrics should we be tracking? Most broadly, I think we want frontier *efficiency* metrics: e.g. FLOP cost of calculation, monetary cost of a FLOP, energy cost of a solar cell, efficiency of chemical synthesis. Would also be good to track more equilibrium metrics, e.g. cybercrime, though these are harder to interpret because they are outcome of a multi-player game. It's interesting to track production of code, software, and academic papers, but it's very difficult to proxy for quality, and that makes those harder to interpret.

5. We don't know expenditure. Ideally we'd want to track the total expenditure on discovery, but that's super hard to get data on (esp. including failed discoveries). Still the data on output is informative.

2107188673381109846.text:
More curves are bending. In mid-August Nate Rush & I posted an analysis of which discovery curves are starting to bend. What's happened since then?

Cyber vulnerabilities: curve is still bent. Discovery of vulnerabilities is accelerating even further, though exploited vulnerabilities remain fairly flat.

Math: curve is further bent. We said there was a likely acceleration for small-scale problems. Since then there has been a claimed Millennium prize resolution, & credible rumors of another. All frequently-updated databases of open problems seem to be proceeding at a rapid rate.

Algorithms: curve is now bending. Two high profile algorithmic competitions have had big curve-bending events: NanoGPT, and the Hutter compression prize. Other frequently-updated series remain relatively unchanged: CIFAR-10, Stockfish, matrix-multiplication exponent.

More observations below.
